name: Annotation that restates its own code
rationale: These rules fire where the text of an annotation can be rebuilt from what it annotates: a trivial comment or a docstring whose first sentence is the function name in prose, an Elixir @doc Parameters block that repeats the head, a narrator sentence announcing what the next line does, a long docstring over a few lines of body, and an explicit type that inference already gives.
invariant: An annotation must carry something the annotated code cannot state for itself, above all the reason the code is as it is.
roles: reason the code is as it is

relations.label: already shows its names, signature and effect
paraphrases it in prose or repeats its type

relations.from: reason the code is as it is
relations.label: is recorded in it

legitimate: Restatement earns its place where the reader is not expected to read the code: a published API docstring that a documentation generator turns into reference for callers, a project or language convention that requires a doc entry on every public member, a line over an opaque idiom whose meaning is not readable, and an explicit type written to pin a widening or to stop an inferred type from drifting with a dependency.

name: Prose banner where a named unit belongs
rationale: Divider bars, section headers, changelog-style section markers and numbered Step 1, Step 2 comments all give a stretch of code a heading in prose instead of extracting it. The rules read the banner as a sign that the body holds several stages and that the author chose a comment over a name.
invariant: A stretch of code distinct enough to deserve a heading must take its name from a code unit that can be called, tested and moved, not from a line of prose above it.

relations.label: is one of several stages inside it
gives it a heading in prose
would carry that name in code

legitimate: A heading is the right tool where extraction is not available: a long declarative literal such as a constants table, a configuration map or a generated data block; file-scope grouping in a language with no unit narrower than the file; and the one conventional line that separates imports from definitions, which marks layout rather than standing in for a function.

name: Author's stance where a fact is owed
rationale: Assuming, presumably, obviously, simply, sorry, hacky, hopefully, might work, and a temp or debug note beside a console.log: each rule matches a comment that grades the code rather than explaining it. The comment shows that the author knew something was uncertain, ugly or temporary, and withholds what a maintainer would need, namely what is unverified or what forced the shape.
invariant: A comment that flags the code as uncertain, obvious, unpleasant or provisional must state the fact behind that judgement: what is not known, what constraint forced the shape, or what would have to change.
roles: maintainer deciding whether to touch the code

relations.label: grades it as doubtful, obvious, shameful or temporary

relations.from: maintainer deciding whether to touch the code
relations.label: can act on what it says

legitimate: The same words are informative once the fact is attached: an assumption comment that names the invariant it rests on and where that invariant is enforced, a hack comment that names the platform bug or deadline forcing it and the condition for removing it, and a hedge that reports a measured uncertainty, such as an undocumented third-party response shape, with the fallback it justifies.
kind_condition: the stance comment does not also state the fact behind its judgement: what is unverified and where the relied-on invariant is enforced, the constraint (platform bug, deadline) that forced the shape and when it can be removed, or the measured uncertainty and the fallback it justifies
kind_judge_reason: Each rule matches a stance word in a comment (assuming/presumably, obviously/simply, sorry/hacky, should work/hopefully, or a debug/temp note beside a console.log) and names a possible fault (unverified assumption, false certainty, self-deprecation, hedging, a log the author knows should go), but such a comment states nothing the code cannot only if it withholds the underlying fact, which no rule checks; the entry's own legitimate case says the same words are informative once that fact is attached, so this is the animation case of the kind test, not a stated family failure (question 1) or a bare word count with no stated fault (question 2).

name: Comment standing in for code never written
rationale: Both rules match prose about work that is absent: add more validation, handle additional cases, can be extended in the future, add your logic here, replace this with your actual implementation, in a real application you would. The comment is the only place the behaviour appears, so it describes an imagined program rather than the delivered one.
invariant: Prose in the source must describe the code that ships; no required behaviour may exist only as a sentence in a comment.

relations.label: names it as something to be added later

legitimate: The same wording is honest over an extension point that is truly optional in code whose present behaviour is complete: a documented hook that a host may override, a template or scaffold distributed to be filled in, or a TODO tied to a tracked ticket with a concrete scope where the unit still meets the contract it advertises.

name: Annotation outliving the thing it points at
rationale: Both rules track an annotation against a referent in the code: an ignore directive or expected-unused tag whose finding is no longer raised, and a header Suppressions entry with no matching directive in the body. The tools decide this by consumption at analysis time, so the fault is the dangling reference and not the wording.
invariant: An annotation that names a specific finding, directive or workaround must have that referent present in the code, and must be removed together with it.

relations.label: asserts that it exists and is accepted
is raised or declared during it
believes a problem is still there and accepted

legitimate: An unconsumed annotation is correct when the referent is real but out of this run's reach: a suppression for a check that is off in this configuration or runs only in a nightly profile, a directive that fires only on another platform, language version or build flag, or a forward-looking suppression added with the rule it anticipates where the project accepts unconsumed entries.

name: Change history kept inside the file
rationale: Version lines, dated or time-relative file headers, and memo phrases such as changed from, moved to, refactored, replaces or formerly put the story of an edit into the source. Each rule reads the file as a record of revisions rather than of the code that now stands there, and detects the tense or the version token rather than a claim about behaviour.
invariant: A comment must describe the code as it now stands; how the code came to be that way belongs to the commit record, which is the only copy that stays true.

relations.label: describes a state the code has left
tells them something about the code in front of them

legitimate: History in the file is right when the past still constrains the present and cannot be recovered from the log: a workaround naming the upstream bug and the version that fixes it, a compatibility shim naming the client release it must outlive, a deprecation carrying a removal date, or a header date required for licence or provenance.

name: Source text written to the authoring session instead of the code reader
rationale: These rules flag text that is a byproduct of the authoring session: meta comments about implementation phases or agent behaviour, comments used to tell the user about changes or to ask them questions, and the chat register of praise, preambles, closing summaries and disclaimers. The text serves one person at one moment and does not document the code. Rules 199 and 202 read the agent's reply rather than the files, so the entry rests on the condition that this register is committed to the source.
invariant: A source comment must document the delivered code for whoever opens the file next, not narrate the authoring session or converse with the user; exchanges with the user belong in the review or chat channel, where they can be answered and closed.

relations.label: narrates it, addresses its user or carries its chat register
is shown by the rule to be committed into the source of
states a durable fact about it
is what annotations explain to them

legitimate: Rules 199 and 202 belong to Annotation Noise only under the added condition, which they do not test, that the praise, preamble or disclaimer is committed to a comment or docstring; in a reply to a person a short preamble or a stated limit is ordinary and can be information. For the in-source rules 023 and 299, an addressed note is fine when its reader is any future maintainer: a header saying the file is generated and which command regenerates it, a pointer to the design document or ticket that fixed the shape, a scaffold instruction meant to be removed on customization, or a warning about an invariant the next editor must keep.

name: Added-comment volume in a change
rationale: This rule counts comment lines added across the changed files, with per-extension comment syntax for about seventy file types, and flags the change once the count passes a limit. It selects a diff for attention by quantity and says nothing about what any single comment says.
invariant: A comment earns its place by what it adds to the code; the number of comments in a change is a signal to look, not a fault in itself.

relations.label: sends the diff to them for judgement

legitimate: A large rise in comment lines is right when a change documents a public interface for the first time, adds module headers a project convention requires, or lands a dense algorithm whose derivation must be written down. The count also misses the opposite case: a change under the threshold can consist entirely of restatement.

name: Informal deprecation note without the formal tag
rationale: The rule fires on prose such as legacy alias, back-compat, deprecated alias or kept for compatibility when no formal deprecation tag accompanies it. What it observes is the absence of a machine-readable tag, not that the prose repeats or misstates anything.
invariant: A deprecation must be declared once in the form the toolchain reads, so that callers are warned where they call and not only where someone happens to read the definition.

relations.label: reaches only a reader who opens the definition
warns them at the call site

legitimate: This counts as annotation noise only under an added condition the rule does not test: that the note repeats a status the code already declares, that the compatibility obligation it describes has ended, or that it names the wrong successor. Where the alias is still kept for callers and no tag exists, the prose is the only record of that obligation and carries information the code does not.
kind_condition: the compatibility obligation the informal note describes has ended, the note names the wrong successor, or the note repeats a deprecation status already declared elsewhere in the code

name: Repeated declaration of a binding already declared
rationale: Both rules report a declaration that re-declares what the same scope already declares: a second import of a module the file already imports, or a second export of a symbol the module already exports. Nothing is reimplemented; the declaration list carries an entry that adds no binding beyond the one already present.
invariant: Each module dependency and each exported symbol is declared once in its scope, so the declaration list is a full and non-overlapping record of what the file takes in and gives out.

relations.label: declares the same symbol a second time
contributes a binding not already there

legitimate: Some repeated declarations are required by the language or the tooling rather than redundant: a type-only import beside a value import of the same module, a side-effect import next to a named one, a default and a named export of one symbol kept for existing importers, or a re-export a public entry point or barrel needs. A deprecated alias kept beside the new name is also a deliberate second declaration.

name: Shared definition restated at every use site
rationale: What is duplicated here is a definition rather than a body: a type or interface shape, a constant, a parameter group, a prop set, a response structure, a closed set of string values, a DTO shape on both sides of a layer boundary. Each site writes the definition out for itself, so the concept has no single declaration that the sites reference and no single place where it can be changed.
invariant: A shape or value that several sites share is declared once, and the sites reference that declaration instead of restating it.

relations.label: writes out its own copy of the same shape or value
declares it once under a name

legitimate: Shapes that agree today but answer to different owners stay separate: a wire or storage contract that must not move when the internal model moves, a type in another bounded context, a test's expected shape written out on purpose so a change in the production type fails the test. A constant name or a string literal that recurs by coincidence (two unrelated TIMEOUT constants, a one-off literal that is not a member of a closed set) carries no shared concept, and the name or literal match that rules 123 and 574 key on needs that confirmation.

name: Repository-level redundancy ratio gate
rationale: The rule reports one number for the whole codebase, the share of functions that are dead or duplicated, and fails when it passes a threshold. The duplicate-function count inside it is why the rule touches Duplication, but the gate names no pair of functions that encode one concept and no copy that should go.
invariant: A duplication finding names the copies involved; a threshold on an aggregate redundancy score selects a codebase for review and is not itself a finding.

relations.label: aggregates dead and duplicate functions over all functions
is compared against it to pass or fail the change
identifies the copies that have to be reconciled

legitimate: A score above the threshold is acceptable where the mass is explained: generated clients, vendored or migrated code, parallel language bindings, a deliberate phase in which old and new implementations run side by side, or a score driven by the dead-code component alone. The aggregate is a fair trend measure; it misleads only when read as a list of duplicates.

name: Name, signature and callee-overlap similarity signals
rationale: These rules select candidates for a duplication review from surface features only: a normalized helper signature shape found in several files, a function name found in several files with different signatures, or sibling functions whose callee sets overlap above a score. None of them compares the implementations, and a detector note says the overlap does not establish duplicate behavior.
invariant: A report of duplication rests on duplicated content, not on a matching name, a signature shape or a count of shared callees.

relations.label: selects it by matching names, signature shapes or shared callees above a count
compares what the implementations actually do
has to read the bodies to decide whether a copy exists

legitimate: The signal carries no defect where a name is a convention met independently in many modules (handle, serialize, validate, a framework hook), where an interface or protocol requires the same signature in every implementation, where same-named functions with different signatures are distinct operations or overloads, and where sibling functions share callees because they use the same helpers for different work.

name: Test cases and setup restated per case
rationale: These rules concern copies inside the test suite: setup and mock wiring written out again in each test file, test bodies that differ only in their literals instead of being parameterized, and the same observable behavior asserted again through another internal path. The suite grows copies without growing its evidence, and one behavior change has to be edited in every copy.
invariant: A behavior is set up and asserted in one place in the suite, and cases that differ only in their data share one body through parameters or a fixture.

relations.label: asserts the same behavior again from its own restated setup
takes its setup and its data from it

legitimate: Repetition earns its place in tests when it is the point: a case written out in full because explicitness makes the expected value readable, a regression test kept independent of the shared fixture so a fixture change cannot hide the bug, or two tests that look alike but pin different contracts (a unit path and an end-to-end path over the same behavior). Setup repeated in two files is also fine before it is clear what the shared fixture should be.

name: Hand-rolled version of a facility that is already provided
rationale: In these rules the implementation that already exists is not a sibling in the diff but a facility the project can call: a standard-library function, a platform primitive, an established library, or infrastructure the codebase itself provides. The new code rebuilds that facility, so the project owns a second implementation of it along with the edge cases the facility already handles.
invariant: A capability that the language, the platform, a library or the codebase already provides is used through that provider rather than written again.

relations.label: already supplies it, maintained outside this change

legitimate: Writing it again is right when the facility does not fit: a requirement it does not meet (a performance budget, a platform or dependency constraint, a licence), semantics that must differ in a documented way, or a dependency too large for what is needed. A thin adapter over the facility is not a reimplementation.

name: Copy-and-modify provenance of a new function
rationale: The rule describes a real failure, a function written by copying a neighbour and editing it, which keeps the neighbour's bounds and null semantics and so misses what the new function was specified to do. That failure is a correctness defect; it is a Duplication failure only under a further condition that the rule does not check.
invariant: A function is derived from what it is specified to do, and the part it shares with a neighbour is reused rather than copied.

relations.label: is produced by copying its body and editing it
is derived from what it has to do
reuses the part the two functions genuinely have in common

legitimate: Condition for Duplication: the copy and its source still encode one concept that must change together, so the shared part should have been extracted and called. Copy-and-modify is not duplication where the edits make the new function a different operation that only started from the same text; the copy is then a correctness risk only. It is also acceptable as an intermediate step when the copy is reconciled with its source before the change is delivered.
kind_condition: The copied function and its source still encode one concept whose shared logic should have been extracted, so they must change together.

name: Second implementation of logic the repository already has
rationale: These rules report that a behavior which already has an implementation in the repository is carried out again elsewhere, whether the second site is a textual or structural clone, a re-created helper of the same shape, a repeated call chain, a re-encoding of the same business rule, query, mapping, validation or dispatch structure under other names, or a duplicate that is also unused. The tools differ in how they recognize sameness (normalized line windows, body hashes, AST structure, semantic comparison); what they report is two bodies that must change together.
invariant: One behavior has one implementation in the repository, and every site that needs it calls that implementation.

relations.label: calls it instead of holding its own copy
changes together with it, under one edit

legitimate: Two bodies may look alike and still be right to keep apart: when they serve different bounded contexts or published versions whose rules are free to diverge, when the resemblance is incidental (short accessors, framework boilerplate, generated or vendored code), when a regulatory or deployment boundary requires independent implementations, or when a deliberate copy buys independence worth more than the shared edit. Repetition is also acceptable while a third occurrence has not yet shown which part is really common.

name: Failure signal dropped before it reaches its owner
rationale: These rules detect a failure signal (a thrown exception, a thrown control-flow signal, a returned error value, or the outcome of an asynchronous task) that is caught, received or spawned and then discarded: empty catches, log-and-continue, bare or broad except, a bound error never narrowed or rethrown, a Next.js redirect caught by try/catch, a Go error assigned to `_`, C# `async void`, a dropped Rust `JoinHandle`, and a change made only to suppress an error. In each case the party that owns the failure never sees it, and execution continues as though the operation succeeded.
invariant: A failure signal raised, returned or spawned by an operation must either be genuinely handled where it is received, so that the caller's promised postcondition holds, or reach the party that owns it; it must not be caught, ignored or detached and then dropped.
legitimate: The handler genuinely recovers so the promised postcondition holds; the operation is optional by contract (best-effort cache warm-up, telemetry flush, cleanup on a path already shutting down); a boundary whose job is to stop every failure (request handler, supervisor loop) reports it on the monitored channel; a catch narrows to the failures it names and lets the rest (such as a framework redirect signal) continue; or a spawned task's failure is observed by another declared owner.

name: Failure disguised as a valid value
rationale: When an operation fails or required data is missing, these rules detect a plausible, success-shaped value put in its place: a `.catch()` returning `null`, `[]` or `{}`, `?? 0` or `?? ""` on required data, chained `.get({}).get()` defaults, and a secret environment variable with a hardcoded fallback. The failure does not vanish from the code path; it becomes data the consumer cannot tell apart from a real result.
invariant: A failure or genuinely missing value must surface to the consumer; it must not be replaced by a default or sentinel that a successful operation could also have produced.

relations.label: signals on error or missing data

legitimate: The default is the documented, domain-correct value for a genuinely optional input whose absence is an expected case rather than a failure, and the consumer is designed to treat it so (an optional display label defaulting to an empty string, a pagination offset defaulting to zero).

name: Error identity or cause chain destroyed in propagation
rationale: These rules keep a failure visible but strip its structured type or cause chain while converting, wrapping or re-raising it: early stringification of an unknown error, Python `raise` without `from`, Rust `.to_string()` or `format!` applied too early, and Go `fmt.Errorf` with `%v` instead of `%w`. Downstream code sees that something failed but can no longer match or trace which failure it was.
invariant: When an error is converted, wrapped or re-raised, its structured identity and cause chain must stay available to the handlers above it.

relations.label: flattens to a string or drops the cause of

legitimate: A human-readable string is derived at a display or serialization boundary (UI message, HTTP response body, operator log line) while the structured error is still propagated or recorded internally.

name: Drop in the count of error-handling constructs in a diff
rationale: This rule compares how many try/except, try/catch, `.catch`, ErrorBoundary and None-check occurrences a non-test file has before and after a change and warns on a decrease. The count is the whole predicate: it names no failure path, and deleting a swallowing catch scores the same as deleting a necessary one.
invariant: A change must not remove the handling that kept a still-fallible operation's failure observable.

relations.label: holds fewer counted error-handling constructs than
shows which failure path lost its propagation to

legitimate: The count falls legitimately when handling is consolidated upward, a swallowing handler is removed so the error propagates, the guarded operation can no longer fail, a None check is replaced by a type that cannot be None, or dead code is deleted.

name: Mixed error mechanisms in one module
rationale: The rule reports a module that signals failure in more than one way at once: exceptions beside error codes, `Result` beside thrown errors, callbacks beside promises. That is a real hazard because a caller usually handles one mechanism, but the rule stops at the inventory and never shows that a failure is in fact lost.
invariant: Where two failure mechanisms meet, the crossing must translate the signal, so that a caller handling one mechanism cannot miss a failure raised through the other.
legitimate: The added condition the rule does not check: the mixture belongs in this family only when some call path crosses from one mechanism to the other without carrying the failure over, so a caller watching one mechanism sees success. Mixing is legitimate when each crossing translates explicitly (a Result-returning wrapper around a throwing library, a promisified callback API) or follows the platform convention (throw for programmer errors, return Result for expected ones).
kind_condition: A call path crosses from one error mechanism to the other without translating the failure, so a caller handling one mechanism sees success while a failure was raised through the other.

name: Error reported on the non-error log channel
rationale: The rule flags `console.log` inside a catch clause. The failure is real, since an error written at info level to stdout is not collected as an error by log processing and alerting, but the match is purely positional: it does not check whether the error object is passed or whether the handler also rethrows or returns a failure.
invariant: A handler that reports a failure by logging must log the error itself on the channel the system treats as its error channel.

relations.label: is passed with message and stack to

legitimate: The added condition the rule does not check: this belongs in this family only when the log line is the handler's whole disposition of the error, so nothing is rethrown or returned. Where the handler rethrows or returns an error value, where the log is only supplementary context, or where the program deliberately routes all output to stdout (a CLI, a container whose stdout is the collected stream, a test harness), the channel choice swallows nothing.
kind_condition: The console.log call is the handler's entire disposition of the error, with nothing rethrown or returned, so the failure is only reported on the non-error channel and never propagated.

name: Declared artifact with no consumer
rationale: These rules resolve references across a file, a module graph or a project and report something a change declares or keeps that nothing else asks for: an import, a top-level declaration, an export, a type, a whole file, a class or enum member, a component, a prop, a component event, a server action, or code that is both duplicated and unused. The kind of artifact differs; the question asked of it does not.
invariant: Every declaration a change leaves in the delivered system must be referenced by at least one other part of that system.
legitimate: The artifact is consumed from outside the analysed repository (a published library surface, a plugin contract, an SDK type), or it is an entry point the framework calls by convention (a route, a layout, a CLI command, a registered hook, a migration script). It is also legitimate when the only reference is one static analysis cannot see, such as a dynamic import, a string-keyed registry, reflection or a build step that generates the call site.

name: Production dependency the shipped runtime never loads
rationale: Both rules find a package that is genuinely imported, so the no-consumer check does not fire, but every import of it is absent from what ships: type-only imports are erased at compile time and test files are not delivered. The manifest therefore states a run-time requirement the running system does not have.
invariant: A package declared as a production dependency must be required by code that ships and runs.

relations.label: declares as required at run time

legitimate: A library that re-exports the package's types in its own public API must keep it where its consumers will install it. The same holds when the package is loaded through a dynamic or plugin resolution the analyser cannot follow, and in a setup where one manifest deliberately serves shipped code and tests together, so the production and development split carries no meaning.

name: Permanently unreachable code
rationale: Statements placed after a return, throw, raise, break or continue, and a branch governed by a literal-constant condition, are executable code that no control path of the delivered system can reach. The question is reachability, not whether anything references the code.
invariant: Every statement and branch left in delivered code must be reachable on some execution path.

relations.label: presents itself as live behaviour to

legitimate: A constant condition can be a deliberate compile-time or build-time switch (a debug flag, a platform constant the bundler folds away), and some unreachable statements are required: an exhaustiveness default, a return after an exit call, or a raise the compiler or linter insists on.

name: Commented-out code retained in source
rationale: The rule flags blocks of real code that were disabled by turning them into comments and left in the file. The compiler never sees them and nothing depends on them; they keep an old version of the code in place of deleting it and leaving the history to version control.
invariant: Code that has been disabled must be deleted from the source, not kept as commented-out text.
legitimate: A short commented example that documents usage (an example call in a docstring), a disabled line in a configuration template that users are meant to switch on, or a brief snippet kept on purpose with a note on why an alternative was rejected.

name: Operation declared with an empty body
rationale: Both rules find a declared operation, a non-trivial function or a React useEffect hook, whose body performs no work. That is a real failure, but whether it is debris or omitted behaviour depends on whether anything expects an effect from the operation, which neither rule checks.
invariant: An operation that performs no work and from which nothing expects an effect should not be declared or registered at all.
legitimate: The finding belongs to Hygiene Debris only on the added condition that nothing expects an effect from the operation, so it can be deleted; if a caller or a stated requirement expects the effect, the empty body is work omitted and presented as done (family I). An empty body is acceptable outright where the slot is mandatory: an abstract or protocol method, an interface conformance, a deliberate no-op default or handler, a pass in an exception subclass, or a useEffect whose purpose is the cleanup function it returns.
kind_condition: nothing expects an effect from the operation, so it can be deleted rather than filled in

name: Debug instrumentation shipped with the change
rationale: A stray print or console call, a bare debugger statement and a console.log carrying an apologetic debug comment are instrumentation the author added to watch a run. None of them is product behaviour, and all are found by matching the statement and then deciding whether the file is production code.
invariant: Output and breakpoints added to observe a run during development must be removed, or replaced by the project's own logging, before the change is delivered.
legitimate: Writing to standard output is the product in a CLI, a build script, a generator or a test reporter, and deliberate operator-facing output or structured telemetry through the project's logger is not debris. A debugger statement is legitimate only in code that never ships, such as a local development harness or a path gated to development builds.

name: Traces of the authoring process delivered as product
rationale: Session planning and scratch files committed to the repository, and markers that a generator left in delivered text (citation tokens, sandbox paths, tracking parameters, placeholder tokens), both come from the act of producing the change rather than from the change itself. Nothing in the delivered system reads them; they differ only in whether the trace is a whole file or a token inside delivered content.
invariant: A change delivers the product only; scratch files and generator markers made while producing it must be removed or resolved before delivery.
legitimate: Design records kept on purpose are not residue: an ADR, a maintained ROADMAP or TODO the team works from, or documentation under docs/. Placeholder text is legitimate in a template or fixture whose job is to be filled in, and in prose that discusses the markers themselves. Where a placeholder stands in for content the document was required to carry, the failure is an incomplete delivery (family I) rather than debris.

name: Edits of a failed fix attempt left in the change
rationale: The rule requires that when an attempted fix fails, all of its edits be reverted at once, and forbids dead code accumulating from abandoned attempts. The leftover edits were written as product code, not as notes or markers, but they contribute nothing to the solution that is delivered.
invariant: Edits made by a failed or abandoned fix attempt must be reverted rather than left in the delivered change.
legitimate: Edits from an attempt that succeeded, edits kept because they are part of the accepted solution, and parts of a failed attempt that are improvements on their own merits (a refactoring, an added test) are not residue; edits are also fine while the attempt is still in progress.

name: Half-wired event channel
rationale: The publisher rule and the subscriber rule are mirror images of one check: match the channel names used at publish sites against those used at subscribe sites. Either way one end is registered and its counterpart is absent, so the wiring exists but carries nothing.
invariant: Each end a change registers on an event channel must have its counterpart in the same system, so that what is published is received and what is listened for can arrive.
legitimate: The counterpart lives outside the analysed code: another service, a separate repository, an external consumer of a documented event contract, a plugin or extension API, or an operator watching a channel by hand. It is also legitimate when the channel name is assembled at run time, so name matching cannot pair the two ends, and when an emit belongs to a public component API whose listeners are written by its users.

name: Migration scaffolding outliving its migration
rationale: The rule reports deprecated symbols, mixed old and new APIs, stale shims, completed migration wrappers and abandoned 'remove later' notes. Read as hygiene, the shim and the deprecated symbol are dead weight left after the move finished, but the rule reports the unfinished case in the same breath and never says which one it found.
invariant: When a migration is finished, the shim, the deprecated symbol and the removal marker that carried the old path are removed with it.
legitimate: The finding belongs to this family only on the added condition that the migration has completed and no caller, published API or still-supported release needs the old path; while old call sites remain, the shim is live compatibility structure and the mixed state is unfinished migration work (families S and I). A deprecation window the project promised to honour, or a shim kept for an external consumer on an older version, is legitimate even with no internal caller left.
kind_condition: the migration has completed and no caller, published API, or still-supported release needs the old path

name: Surplus repeated declaration of one binding
rationale: Importing the same module twice and exporting the same symbol twice break one rule of bookkeeping: the first declaration already established the binding, so the second adds nothing and only creates a second place to keep in step. Both are found by grouping a file's declarations by the name they bind.
invariant: A module brought into a file, or a symbol sent out of it, is declared once.

relations.label: establishes a second time with no added effect

legitimate: A toolchain can require the split: a separate type-only import next to a value import, or a side-effect-only import kept alongside a named one. On the export side, publishing a symbol under a deliberate second alias, or re-exporting it from a barrel as well as from its own module, is a chosen public surface rather than a slip.

name: Suppression annotation that outlived the condition it covered
rationale: A suppression comment whose finding no longer exists and a header Suppressions entry whose directive was deleted are the same bookkeeping failure: the annotation was paired with something in the code, that something went away, and the annotation stayed. Both tools find it by pairing annotations against the body and reporting those with no partner.
invariant: An annotation that exists only to cover a condition in the code must be removed when that condition is removed.
legitimate: A suppression may be kept deliberately for a finding that comes and goes, for instance in conditionally compiled or generated code, after a dependency update, or with an analyser whose result depends on build order, and a header entry may be held through a staged cleanup with a note saying so. An unconsumed suppression is also harmless when it was written for a different tool or a stricter configuration than the one that ran.

name: Redundancy ratio gate
rationale: The rule scores dead functions plus duplicate functions as a fraction of all functions and fails when the fraction passes a configured threshold. It selects a codebase for attention by a ratio and does not name an artifact or the obligation any particular function breaks.
invariant: The share of functions that are dead or duplicated should stay under the configured fraction of all functions.
legitimate: The ratio runs high for sound reasons: generated or vendored code counted in both terms, a library whose wide public API looks uncalled from inside the repository, platform shims that are duplicates by necessity, a codebase in active migration, or a small codebase where a few functions swing the fraction. A ratio under the threshold also says nothing about whether real debris is present.

name: Hallucinated or nonexistent API reference
rationale: These rules detect code that references imports, methods, attributes, or function signatures that do not exist in the target language or library. Cross-language contamination (JS methods in Python, Java methods in Python, etc.) and framework-confused imports (Next.js APIs imported from React) share the same broken obligation: the code calls something that is not there.
invariant: Every module, API, member or symbol the code names must exist in the environment where the code will run.
legitimate: Optional imports guarded by try/except for graceful degradation, development-time type stubs not executed at runtime, framework-specific reexports that alias the original API, and version-conditional imports with proper fallbacks.

name: Implementation taken from a neighbour instead of from the specification
rationale: This rule targets code written by copying a similar function and editing it, and the bounds and null-handling errors that travel with it. What the rule identifies is the provenance; whether the result actually departs from the specification it is presented as implementing is left unchecked.
invariant: An implementation must be derived from the specification it is presented as satisfying.

relations.label: relies on it for the specified behavior
carries over its bounds and null semantics

legitimate: The added condition is that the copied code's behavior really does differ from what was specified. Copying a neighbouring function and adapting it correctly is ordinary practice and misrepresents nothing; the copy is also legitimate where the two cases share one specification, in which case the duplication, not the integrity, is the issue.
kind_condition: the copied implementation actually departs from the specification it is presented as satisfying

name: Claim or value presented as established without evidence
rationale: Each rule flags a claim or value presented as true that is not backed by fresh, direct evidence: completion claims without command output, figures without a baseline, uncited claims, invented paths, keys or versions, and the general no-fabrication and phantom-fix constraints.
invariant: A claim of completion, correctness or performance, or a concrete value written into the work, must be backed by evidence obtained and verified in the current run, not asserted, assumed or invented.
legitimate: A claim or figure accompanied by the fresh command output, measured baseline or citation that substantiates it; an estimate or example value that is explicitly labelled as such.

name: Substitute delivered in place of the requested work
rationale: Both rules target a response that satisfies the form of the request while leaving its substance undone: answering a defect report with tests, documentation or an absence check instead of a code change, and meeting a stated metric in a way that defeats what the metric was measuring. The acceptance signal is produced; the requested work is not.
invariant: A change presented as answering a requirement or finding must actually fulfill it, not deliver another artifact or a gamed metric that only produces the acceptance signal.

relations.label: is delivered in place of it

legitimate: A substitute the requester accepts once it is named as one, for instance a regression test added after showing that the reported behavior is in fact correct; and cases where the metric genuinely is the goal rather than a proxy for it.

name: Placeholder, sample value or deferral marker left in a delivered artifact
rationale: Each rule flags a stand-in for absent or unfinished work left inside something presented as delivered: TODO/FIXME markers, vague specifications, filler comments, AI handoff phrases, coming-soon headings, Lorem ipsum and demo values, and a hardcoded fallback behind a secret environment variable that makes the system look configured.
invariant: An artifact presented as delivered must contain the finished content and the real values it depends on, not a placeholder, sample value or marker that stands in for work still owed.
legitimate: A tracked TODO tied to an issue or owner, a transparent future-work heading that makes no claim the work is done, and example configuration or seed data declared as such (.env.example, a demo seed script) or a local default behind a guard that refuses to start in production.

name: Test that passes without examining the production behavior
rationale: Both rules catalogue tests whose green result is manufactured inside the test: the fixture creates the end state, the system under test is mocked away, the expected value is recomputed with the same formula, or there is no assertion at all. Unlike a disabled check, these tests are counted in the suite and read as evidence.
invariant: A test that passes must do so because the production behavior it names is correct, and it must be able to fail when that behavior is wrong.

relations.label: is read as evidence about it
passes whether or not it holds

legitimate: Smoke or import tests, and compile-only or type-level checks, when they are named for what they do and the behavior itself is covered elsewhere; and a fixture standing in for an external system while the assertion still targets production logic.

name: Description that contradicts the system it describes
rationale: These rules all compare prose about the system with the system: a comment against adjacent code, doc tags against a signature, a sample against the real API, documentation against the changed code, and documented paths, versions and counts against the repository. Each failure is a statement about the software that is false, which misleads the reader more than silence would.
invariant: Every statement a description makes about the system must be true of the system as delivered.

relations.label: acts on it instead of reading the code

legitimate: Text explicitly scoped to another version or to the past (changelogs, release notes, architecture decision records), and a comment that records intent, rationale or a known deviation rather than describing current behavior.

name: Operation with an empty or canned body
rationale: These rules all flag a callable that occupies the place of a finished operation while its body does nothing or hands back a fixed answer: empty bodies, not-implemented raises and panics, constant returns, and classes where most methods are such bodies.
invariant: An operation presented as implemented must actually perform its specified work.

relations.label: calls it as the finished implementation
advertises it by name and signature
returns an empty or canned result anyway

legitimate: Abstract methods, protocol and interface declarations, and overridable hooks whose documented behavior is to do nothing (null objects, default no-op handlers, a deliberately empty cleanup). There the empty body is the behavior, not a missing one.

name: Part of the specified work never implemented
rationale: These rules compare a stated set of obligations with the implementation and find part of the set absent: variants of a closed domain left unhandled, call sites never moved to the new API, specified transitions with no handler, plan tasks and mitigations not built. The whole is reported as delivered and no marker records the part that is not.
invariant: Every case, step and task the specification or plan requires must be realized in the implementation before the work is reported as delivered.

relations.label: presents partial coverage as the whole

legitimate: A requirement explicitly cut from this change and recorded as out of scope; a migration staged on purpose with the remaining call sites tracked and the old path still supported; a partial match whose remaining variants are unreachable by construction and asserted to be so.

name: Confidence vocabulary in prose
rationale: These rules select prose by its confidence markers: hedges such as assuming, presumably, should work, and certainty words such as obviously, clearly, trivially. The word list picks out text to look at; none of these rules establishes that the behavior described is in fact unverified or that completion is misrepresented.
invariant: Prose about the code should express no more and no less certainty than the author has grounds for.

relations.label: describes it with a hedge or a certainty marker
is pointed at it by the keyword match

legitimate: A hedge that honestly records a limit ('may be null here, not yet verified') is the disclosure this family wants, not a defect; and 'simply' or 'obviously' in an explanation of something genuinely simple carries no claim about the software at all.

name: Public surface hidden from the generated documentation
rationale: This rule counts @doc false attributes on public functions and reports a module that hides much of what it exposes. The failure it names is real, that readers of the API cannot see a surface callers can reach, but the rule cannot tell whether those functions are part of the API the project presents as supported.
invariant: The documentation generated for a module must cover the surface the project presents as that module's API.
legitimate: The added condition is that the hidden functions belong to the surface the project presents as documented and supported. @doc false on functions that are public only for macro expansion or for use inside the application, which the project does not offer to callers, is the intended use of the attribute and claims nothing false.
kind_condition: the hidden functions belong to the surface the project presents as documented and supported

name: Pass obtained by neutralizing the check
rationale: These rules watch for a change that produces a green signal by acting on the checker rather than on the code: weakening or deleting assertions, skipping tests, turning off compiler warnings and nullability, editing lint configuration, overriding a dependency constraint, and suppressing an error signal. The gate still reports success, so the property it existed to protect quietly stops being checked.
invariant: A gate may only be passed by making the code satisfy the check; the check itself must not be weakened, disabled or reconfigured to produce the pass.

relations.label: is read as evidence that it holds

legitimate: Retiring a check the project has decided no longer applies, with the decision recorded and reviewed; a suppression that carries its justification and is scoped to the one line it covers; and deleting a test whose behavior was deliberately removed from the product.

name: Known gap or assumption kept out of the report
rationale: These rules concern what the report leaves out rather than what it asserts: areas that were not verified, assumptions the implementation rests on, and material facts such as a known failing edge case. Everything stated may be true, and the reader still takes partial work for complete work.
invariant: A report must disclose the gaps, assumptions and known defects of the work alongside its results.

relations.label: decides on the strength of it
lets partial work read as complete

legitimate: Gaps already recorded where the reader is pointed at them (an issue tracker, a risk register referenced in the report), and omissions of what the agreed scope plainly excludes, which no reader would read as covered.

name: Integration point with only one end built
rationale: Both rules find a connection where one side is fully written and the other side never exists: a parameter or field no caller ever passes, and an injected key no ancestor ever provides. Reading either file suggests a finished feature; the feature can never run, because nothing joins the two ends.
invariant: A declared integration point must have both ends present in the delivered system: whatever one side requests, some other side must supply.
legitimate: An extension point published for consumers outside this repository, a parameter kept for backwards compatibility, and a provider registered dynamically at runtime (a plugin, a test harness, a DI container) that static analysis of the tree cannot see.

name: Safeguard present in the source and inert where it runs
rationale: These rules each flag a mechanism that reads as a guarantee and provides none: an assert the interpreter discards under optimization, a hash or validator that offers no protection, a boundary directive the framework ignores because of where it sits. The mechanism is visible, which is why nobody looks for the guarantee again.
invariant: A mechanism presented as enforcing a property must actually enforce it in the configuration the code runs in.

relations.label: counts the property as guarded because it is there

legitimate: An assert used deliberately as a development-time sanity check where the real enforcement lives elsewhere; a fast non-cryptographic hash used for cache keys or checksums rather than for secrets; a directive in a file whose boundary the framework establishes by another route.

name: Dependency used but never declared
rationale: Both rules compare what the change consumes (an imported package, an invoked binary) against what the manifest declares, and report the use that is nowhere declared. The package may well exist; what is missing is the declaration that makes the change reproducible.
invariant: Everything the change needs at build or run time must be declared in the project manifest, so the change works in an environment built from that manifest alone.
legitimate: Packages the runtime or standard library supplies, peer dependencies the consuming application is expected to declare, workspace packages resolved by a monorepo root manifest, and type-only imports that are erased before the code ships.

name: Declared interface not honored by the code behind it
rationale: These rules compare a machine-readable contract with what the implementation actually delivers across the boundary: a response type against the payload the producer sends, field names against the names each layer passes on, an overridden member against the contract the base type advertises. Consumers compile cleanly against a promise that is broken at runtime.
invariant: The interface a consumer is given must be honored by the implementation on the other side of it.

relations.label: promises a shape or a capability
is written and type-checked against it
breaks it when the call is actually made

legitimate: A subtype documented as supporting part of the interface where callers test for support first; and a boundary where the declared type is deliberately wider than any single producer and the consumer validates the payload at runtime.

name: Change beyond the requested scope
rationale: These rules all describe one failure: the delivered change contains edits, additions or concerns that the task did not ask for. Whether the agent builds an unrequested feature or abstraction (083), answers a fix request with edits to unrelated files (206), smuggles a behaviour change into a change presented as a refactor (296), or tidies, reorganizes or edits comments outside the task (298), the broken obligation is the same: every modified region must trace back to the request.
invariant: Every region the change modifies or adds traces to the task the user actually requested, and a change presented as behaviour-preserving carries no unrequested behavioural edit.
legitimate: The extra edit is acceptable when the request itself authorizes it (the task asked for the cleanup, refactor, reorganization or migration), when it is a mechanically required consequence of the requested change (a rename that must propagate, callers of a changed interface, an import the new call needs, a restructuring that makes the fix possible), or when the project convention or the user explicitly accepts the broadened scope and the change description declares it.

name: Measured growth as a stand-in for unrequested scope
rationale: All three rules measure how much larger the code got and flag the number: a positive net non-test line delta over the diff (204), a file more than a fifth above its last daily baseline (483), net growth or churn multiplied by complexity over a time window (107). None of them reads the request, so growth the task demanded scores exactly like growth nobody asked for.
invariant: Growth in the delivered code must be accounted for by the request, not merely kept small.
legitimate: Any request that adds a feature, a test suite, a generated client or a vendored dependency makes the code bigger, and a file under active development grows every day it is worked on. The numbers are usable as a review queue or a trend to watch; they are not a finding by themselves.

name: Conjunction in the commit subject as a stand-in for mixed concerns
rationale: Rule 421 reads the commit subject and nothing else, matching the word 'and' on a word boundary. It is a keyword stand-in for the obligation that a commit carry one concern: the conjunction may join two concerns that should have been two commits, or it may just be ordinary prose about one. It inspects no diff and no request.
invariant: A commit should contain one concern that traces to the request, and its subject should say which one.

relations.label: is read to confirm there is only one

legitimate: Plenty of single-purpose subjects carry the word: 'handle null and empty input', 'rename find-and-replace helper', 'document the retry and backoff settings'. The converse is just as common, a commit that really does two things and whose subject mentions only the first, so the keyword is neither necessary nor sufficient for the real failure.

name: Abandoned attempt left in the delivered change
rationale: Rule 540 is about the agent's own discarded work rather than about code it was never asked to touch. Lines written for a fix attempt that failed were never taken back out, so they travel with the attempt that did work and widen the delivered change beyond the accepted solution.
invariant: When a fix attempt fails, its edits must be reverted before the change is delivered, so the change holds only the accepted solution.
legitimate: An abandoned attempt sometimes leaves something the task wants in its own right: a test that reproduces the bug, code the final fix turned out to need, a comment recording why the obvious route does not work. Keeping those deliberately and documenting it is not this failure; nor does it apply while the attempt is still live and nothing has been delivered.

name: Placeholder name in place of the domain term
rationale: The four rules catch a name that fills the naming slot without naming anything: a role word with a counter (helper_1, data2), a blocklisted filler verb phrase (process_data, handle_response), a grab-bag module name (utils, helpers), or a function body made mostly of one- and two-character identifiers. The artifact differs (variable, parameter, function, module) but in each case the reader cannot recover from the name which domain concept the thing stands for.
invariant: Every named artifact must denote the specific domain concept it holds, so that the concept can be read off the name without reading the implementation.
legitimate: A contentless or very short name is right when the code is genuinely generic over the concept or the scope makes it unambiguous: a type parameter, loop indices and coordinates (i, j, k, x, y), a lambda argument in a one-line pipeline, established abbreviations the project uses (id, db, err), or a utility module that the project's own convention names utils and keeps to one documented purpose.

name: Name restates the context it already sits in
rationale: Both rules concern names that are long because they repeat what the enclosing module, class, function or type already states, not because they make a finer distinction. Rule 129 catches redundant context prefixes and type suffixes (getUserDataFromDatabase, currentUserAuthenticationStatusBoolean); rule 132 catches tokens repeated from the enclosing scope (user_update_user_profile in UserService).
invariant: A name must add the distinction its enclosing scope does not already make, and must not repeat what the scope or type already supplies.
legitimate: Repetition is right when the scope is not visible at the use site: an exported symbol read unqualified in another module, a flat C-style or global namespace, a name the project's public API spells in full, a multi-word domain term the project already uses, or two names in one scope that only the longer form tells apart.

name: Departure from the naming convention in force
rationale: These rules take the project itself, at some scope, as the standard: the rest of the same file (131), the other names in the directory (128), the whole codebase (115), a per-language file-name casing rule (384), or a declared per-directory placement rule (564). In each the added artifact's surface form or location is not the one the project uses for artifacts of its kind, so the form of a name stops predicting anything. Identifier, file name and file location are artifact types of one obligation.
invariant: An added identifier, file name or file location must take the form the project already uses for that kind of artifact.
legitimate: A different form is correct when another convention governs the artifact: generated code, vendored third-party sources, a name a framework or wire format fixes (HTTP headers, environment variables, serialised keys), migration or fixture directories, files such as __init__.py, Makefile or Dockerfile, and a documented project-wide migration in which new code takes the target convention.

name: One field under diverging names across layers
rationale: The rule is about the correspondence between the ends of a data path, not about a local convention: the storage layer, the API response and the client types each name the same field their own way, and the mapping between the forms is applied at some boundaries and not at others, which shows as field-access errors. There is no single surrounding standard to match; what fails is that one concept no longer has one term, or one reliable translation, along its path.
invariant: A field must keep one term, or one consistently applied mapping between terms, at every architectural boundary it crosses.

relations.label: maps the name at every boundary
reads under a form the producer never emits

legitimate: Per-layer conventions are expected (snake_case columns, camelCase JSON, PascalCase types); the divergence is acceptable whenever the translation is declared once and applied everywhere, by a serialiser configuration, generated client types or a schema the layers share, so that no consumer spells a key by hand.

name: Domain term misspelled at its declaration
rationale: The rule flags identifiers whose spelling is wrong at the declaration site, confirmed by comparing comparable identifiers in the repository. The name can pick the right concept and follow the right convention and still spell the term wrongly, so the concept exists under two spellings, stops being one searchable word, and the typo propagates to every reference.
invariant: An identifier must spell its domain term as the term is spelled by comparable identifiers in the repository.
legitimate: The apparent misspelling is right when it is the project's or the domain's own spelling: an established abbreviation or acronym, a British or American variant the repository has settled on, correct jargon that looks like a typo, a field name fixed by an external schema or API, or a historical typo kept for compatibility in a public API or stored data.

name: Raw literal selected by size or format
rationale: Both rules select inline literals for review by their surface form: numeric literals by digit count (over 1000 or four or more digits) or by more than three distinct non-trivial literals per function (198), and CSS values by pixel size, hex, rgba() or hsl() format (372). Neither checks that the value has a domain meaning or that the project has a named constant or design token for it, so they select code rather than state that the obligation to name the value is broken.
invariant: A value with domain meaning should be referred to through the named constant or design token the project gives it, not inlined as an anonymous literal.

relations.label: contains a literal selected by size or format

legitimate: A literal is the right text when the value has no name to carry: 0, 1 and -1 as structural values, a mathematical constant in a formula, the definition of the named constant itself, a value used once where its meaning is evident, a one-off value in a test or fixture, a value in a declarative configuration file whose key names it, and a style value in a prototype or a file outside the design system.

name: Decorative glyphs in source text
rationale: Emoji in code and comments (130) and decorative typographic characters such as em dashes, smart quotes, ellipses and arrows (321) are one finding under two character sets: prose ornament carried into a source file. Neither rule compares the characters with what the project's own sources contain, so neither establishes the mismatch with repository vocabulary that family L requires.
invariant: Source files and comments should keep to the character register the project's own sources use, without decorative or typographic glyphs.
legitimate: The added condition the rules do not check: the finding belongs to this family only if the project's existing sources avoid these characters for this purpose. Where they do not, the glyph is correct: emoji and typographic punctuation in user-facing strings, localisation data, documentation and Markdown, CLI output the project deliberately decorates, identifiers in a non-ASCII natural language, documented Unicode operators in scientific code, and test data that exercises Unicode handling.
kind_condition: the project's own existing sources avoid these emoji and typographic characters for this purpose, so the introduced glyph lies outside the project's character register

name: Runtime re-establishment of an already-assured value property
rationale: The rules flag a coercion, a null or type check, a parameter validation, or a recomputation applied to a value whose type, nullability, validity or result is already settled at that point, either by the type system or by a trusted caller or upstream boundary. The source of the guarantee differs between the rules, but in each case the operation cannot change the outcome because the property already holds.
invariant: A check, coercion or recomputation may only establish a property of a value that is not already assured at that point in the code, whether the assurance comes from the type system or from a trusted caller or boundary.
roles: upstream guarantee (type system or validating caller)

relations.from: upstream guarantee (type system or validating caller)
relations.label: already fixes its type, nullability, validity or computed result
re-tests, re-coerces or re-derives the settled property
would deliver the value without the property and so justify the check

legitimate: The check is the real guarantee at a trust boundary where the static type or the caller's validation cannot be relied on: a public or exported API callable by untrusted or untyped code, an HTTP or CLI entry point, a deserializer, parsed JSON or values typed as any or unknown, data read from a file or database, or code reached after an unsafe cast. It is also right when the project deliberately asserts the invariant as a precondition contract, or when the compiler does not run in a mode that proves the property.

name: Error handling that reproduces default propagation
rationale: A catch that only rethrows the caught error unchanged, and a try/catch around code that cannot throw, both add a handling layer that changes nothing: the runtime already carries any failure to the caller, so removing the construct would leave observable behaviour unchanged.
invariant: An error-handling construct must enclose code that can fail and must change what the caller observes when it fails, beyond what default error propagation already provides.

relations.label: already delivers any failure of the enclosed code
intercepts failures without adding handling (bare rethrow, or nothing can throw)

legitimate: The catch does work when it logs with context, wraps or translates the error into a type the caller's contract names, recovers, or releases a resource on the way out. A try/catch around apparently safe code is justified when the called code can throw in ways the local source does not show, such as a dynamic import, an untyped dependency, a caller-supplied callback or resource exhaustion.

name: Fallback access for an input shape that is already fixed
rationale: A chain of dict gets that defaults to an empty container at each level, and a lookup that tries the atom key and then the string key, both keep a second access path for a form of the data that the input contract or a normalizing boundary has already excluded, so the accessor repeats a shape guarantee that already holds.
invariant: A data accessor must read the shape that the producing boundary guarantees, and may carry a default or an alternative key only for a form that can really arrive.
roles: accessor with default or alternative key

relations.label: already fixes its key form and required fields

relations.from: accessor with default or alternative key
relations.label: handles a missing or alternative shape that cannot occur

relations.to: accessor with default or alternative key
relations.label: would reach it and justify the fallback

legitimate: The fallback is real work in an adapter that genuinely receives both shapes (decoded JSON with string keys and internal structs with atom keys, or old and new payloads during a migration), for raw external data with no validated schema, or for a sparse structure in which the absent field is a meaningful state and the default is the intended value for absence.
kind_condition: the input data shape is already fixed by an upstream contract or normalizing boundary, so only one key form or nesting depth can arrive

name: Look-before-you-leap test before an operation that reports the condition
rationale: The rule matches eight Python shapes in which a condition (key present, attribute present, path exists, non-empty, not None, numeric string, non-zero divisor, isinstance) is tested just before the operation that would itself report it. This is redundant guarding only under the added condition that something already settles the tested state at that point, which the rule does not check.
invariant: A precondition test before an operation must guard a condition that can actually fail at that point; where a reliable guarantee already settles the condition, the test duplicates it.

relations.label: already settles it, which the rule does not establish

legitimate: Added condition for this family: the tested state must already be fixed at that point by a type, a validating caller or a prior normalization. Without it the test is ordinary control flow (the key may be absent, the divisor may be zero) and the branch is intended behaviour. An EAFP style preference is not a duplicated guarantee, the exists-before-open form is a time-of-check to time-of-use race rather than excess, and an isinstance guard is required where a union type must be narrowed.
kind_condition: the tested state is already settled at that point by a type, a validating caller, or a prior normalization, so the precondition check duplicates an existing guarantee

name: Directory population counts
rationale: These rules count files and child directories to pick directories out for review: a fanout above the sibling median, a majority of tiny files, more than twenty files or ten subdirectories. A count cannot show whether the grouping matches a concern.
invariant: A directory should hold the files of one concern, at a granularity that helps navigation.

relations.label: judges whether its files share a concern

legitimate: Flat directories are normal for route trees, migrations, fixtures, icons and generated clients, where the files are peers and further grouping only adds depth. Many small files are also right where each is one component with its own test.

name: Change-history risk score
rationale: These rules combine a complexity measure with recent growth or churn, and in one case with ownership signals, to rank files and functions; one of them reports any file that grew by a fifth since the baseline. History prioritizes attention and says nothing about which structure is unnecessary.
invariant: Complexity should not accumulate in the code that is changed most often.
legitimate: High churn over complex code is the expected signature of active feature work, and growth is the normal signature of an accepted large change. The measures also mislead on young repositories, bulk reformatting and vendored code.

name: Reinvented infrastructure
rationale: Each rule targets code that reimplements a facility the codebase or platform already provides: new utility scaffolding beside existing helpers, a GenServer used as a key-value store where Agent or ETS exists, and a custom implementation of established library functionality.
invariant: New code must reuse an existing codebase or platform facility rather than build a parallel mechanism for the same job.
legitimate: The existing facility does not meet a specific requirement (performance, API shape, dependency constraints), or the custom code is so small that the dependency on the existing facility costs more than it saves.

name: Effect cycle for derived state
rationale: The rule targets a React useEffect whose body only calls setState. The derived value could be computed during render or memoized; instead an effect and a second render are interposed between the source state and the value.
invariant: Derived state must be computed from its source during rendering, not synchronized into a second state through an effect.

relations.label: copies into a second state after render

legitimate: The update must run after render because it depends on something only an effect can observe, such as a DOM measurement or focus, or the effect also performs a real external synchronization.

name: Fallback wording in the agent's own text
rationale: A single rule, a pre-write hook matching phrases that announce a fallback, a shim or an environment-specific patch. It fires on an intention before any code exists, so it observes wording and never a delivered structure.
invariant: A change should repair the path it is tempted to work around rather than add a layer beside it.
legitimate: Fallbacks are often the right answer: a documented default when optional configuration is absent, a compatibility path during a dated migration, a degraded mode when an optional dependency is missing. The phrases also appear when the agent describes existing code or explains why it will not add a workaround.

name: Variation point with no variation
rationale: These rules flag structure whose purpose is to let something differ, where nothing differs: an interface with one implementation, a factory with one output, a class with no state or one method, a generic bound wider than any instantiation, abstraction built for a requirement that has not arrived, and compatibility structure whose migration is over.
invariant: A boundary or variation point must be exercised by the system as it is delivered.
legitimate: A variation point is justified before anything varies when something outside the repository depends on it: a published plugin contract, an interface implemented by a test double or a second runtime, an abstract base for third-party implementors, or a shim an announced deprecation window still requires. Rule 092 belongs here only when the migration is finished; while callers still need the old API, the compatibility structure is not unused.

name: Code outside the place the architecture assigns it
rationale: These rules compare where code sits and what it depends on with the layers, boundaries and placement conventions the project declares or implies: imports that run upward or across a denied boundary, shared code reaching into tools, a contract defined beside its implementation instead of its consumer, a function whose purpose does not match its file, and a file in a directory its conventions forbid.
invariant: Code must reside in, and depend only on, the locations that the project's declared or inferred layers, boundaries and placement rules permit for it.

relations.label: assigns a purpose and an allowed direction to
sits in a place whose purpose it does not share
runs in a direction forbidden by

legitimate: A crossing or placement is acceptable when it is a recorded exception in the boundary configuration, when an inversion seam makes a seemingly upward edge legal, when the platform fixes the location of a file, or when the placement rule is out of date with a layout the project has since chosen.

name: Responsibility not co-located with what changes with it
rationale: These rules flag a split between a responsibility and the unit that should hold it: a method that works on another object's data, classes reaching into each other's internals, a class holding data whose behavior lives elsewhere, a class changed for unrelated reasons, a change that must touch many files, feature logic cut along technical layers, and a generically named module that collects unrelated functions.
invariant: Each responsibility, with the data and behavior that change together, must live in one cohesive unit, and each unit must hold one responsibility.

relations.label: is spread across or reaches into

legitimate: Cross-object access is the unit's defined job (a serializer, mapper, visitor or report), the data holder is an inert transfer object by design, the spread is a cross-cutting concern handled by an agreed mechanism, or the shared edits are a mechanical rename. A module of genuinely cross-domain primitives whose name says what they are is not a grab-bag.

name: Subtype breaks its supertype contract
rationale: The rule flags a subclass that overrides a method to signal not-implemented or unsupported, or that strengthens preconditions or weakens postconditions, so it can no longer stand in for its parent.
invariant: A subtype must honor its supertype's contract and remain substitutable wherever the supertype is expected.
legitimate: The base type explicitly declares the operation optional, or the hierarchy documents the narrowing as part of its contract.

name: Size and complexity measure above a limit
rationale: These rules select a function, class or file by counting its lines, parameters, members, nesting, paths, cyclomatic or cognitive complexity, Halstead measures, divider comments, complexity against coverage, or the concentration of complexity, and comparing the number with a threshold. None of them says which structure is unnecessary.
invariant: A unit's size and decision load should follow from the one responsibility it carries.

relations.label: judges which structure it should not hold

legitimate: Essential complexity has to live somewhere: a parser, a state machine, a protocol decoder, generated code, data tables and a cohesive module with a wide single-purpose API exceed these limits in their clearest form. The scores also move with style, since guard clauses and early returns change the count without changing the design.

name: Framework boundary directive that does not match the code
rationale: These rules flag client/server boundary directives in React Server Components that do not describe the module: 'use client' on a file using no client APIs, a directive placed where it has no effect, and a barrel that mixes client and server modules under one import.
invariant: A framework boundary directive must be placed where it takes effect and must match the runtime needs of the code it covers.

relations.label: matches the actual needs reported to

legitimate: The directive is required by a parent module or framework convention even though the file itself calls no client API.

name: Route identity conflict
rationale: Both rules target App Router structures where two route definitions collide: two handler files resolving to one URL, and sibling dynamic segments at one depth using different parameter names.
