invariant: Each URL path must resolve to exactly one handler, and sibling dynamic segments must share one parameter name.
legitimate: Route groups that intentionally share a path with different layouts, as the framework documents.

name: Test structure mirrors production internals
rationale: The rule flags test organization that mirrors production's class and method layout and asserts one behavior through several internal paths, so a behavior-preserving refactor breaks the suite.
invariant: Test organization must follow observable behavior, not production's internal structure.
legitimate: A per-class test file that matches production is fine when it still asserts behavior through the public interface.

name: Orchestration chain without an aggregating unit
rationale: The rule flags service-to-service call chains longer than three hops (A calls B calls C calls D), read as a sign that no unit composes the flow and each service hands the request on.
invariant: A multi-service flow must be composed by one orchestrating unit rather than relayed along a chain of services.
legitimate: A deep chain is correct when each hop is a separate bounded context that owns its step, or when the flow is a deliberate pipeline or saga with its own coordinator elsewhere.

name: Library unit taking a decision that belongs to its host
rationale: Each rule flags a unit meant to be imported reaching past its own scope: ending the process, changing the import path, initializing at import time, mutating module-global state, fetching collaborators from a global registry, or choosing its own logging mechanism.
invariant: A library unit must take its state and collaborators from its caller and leave process-wide decisions to the entry point.
legitimate: These actions belong in the entry point itself: a CLI main, a cmd/ program, a test harness, a one-file script. A process-wide singleton is fine when the entry point creates it and the library only receives it, and framework plugin autodiscovery can require registration at import time.

name: Pattern not used elsewhere in the repository
rationale: The rule compares a change with the repository's existing patterns, naming, error handling, logging and test style in one check. Only part of that is structural, and the rule does not separate which part it found.
invariant: A new component must be integrated through the structure the repository already uses for components of its kind.

relations.label: now has to maintain two of

legitimate: The added condition for this family is that the mismatch is structural, such as a hand-written client beside generated ones, rather than vocabulary or style. A departure is also right when the new pattern is the stated replacement in a migration, or when the established pattern cannot serve the case.
kind_condition: the pattern mismatch involves structural integration rather than naming or stylistic conventions

name: Dependency-graph shape above a limit
rationale: These rules measure the shape of a dependency, inheritance or render graph (fan-out, coupling between objects, inheritance depth and width, distance from the main sequence, modularity, unstable coupling, propagation cost, render fan-in) and gate on the number. The measurement selects an architecture for review instead of naming an edge that should not be there.
invariant: The dependency graph should let each unit be changed and understood without reasoning about much of the rest.

relations.label: names the edge that should not exist

legitimate: A hub with high fan-in or fan-out is often correct by design: a shared domain type, a logging facade, a design-system component used on every screen, a framework base class. The scores are also sensitive to packaging, and a deep hierarchy can mirror a real domain taxonomy.

name: Required dependency with no provider
rationale: Both rules trace a declared need back through the callers or the ancestor tree and find nothing that satisfies it: a parameter or option field that no caller ever passes, and an inject or getContext key that no ancestor provides.
invariant: A dependency point a unit declares must be supplied on every path that reaches that unit.
legitimate: The provider arrives in the same change, or the dependency is genuinely optional and its default is the intended behavior. Static analysis also misses providers installed dynamically, through a plugin registry or a test harness.

name: Computation and effects interleaved
rationale: Both rules target functions or loops where pure computation is tangled with I/O, input interpretation or side effects: parsing mixed with execution inside a loop, and business calculation mixed with database calls, HTTP requests or logging.
invariant: Pure computation must be separable from I/O and side effects, so that each phase can be called, tested and understood on its own.
legitimate: The computation is a single expression feeding an I/O call, where separating the phases would add indirection without aiding comprehension or testing.

name: Unmodeled data clump
rationale: The rule targets the same group of parameters appearing in three or more method signatures, a domain concept that travels as loose values instead of a type.
invariant: A parameter group that recurs across signatures must be modeled as one cohesive type.
legitimate: The parameters co-occur by coincidence and represent different concepts in different signatures.

name: Caller navigating through a collaborator's internals
rationale: Both rules flag call or attribute chains that walk several links through objects the caller never received (a.b().c().d()), with one implementation filtering fluent, builder, module-qualified and AST-traversal chains.
invariant: A unit must use only the interface of its immediate collaborators and must not depend on the structure behind them.
legitimate: Long chains are the interface itself in fluent builders and query DSLs, and walking is the point for structures a caller is meant to traverse: an AST, a DOM, a parsed document, a configuration tree. Module-qualified access is a path through namespaces, not through objects.

name: Expression step that cannot change the result
rationale: Each rule flags a construct inside an expression or statement whose removal leaves the same value: an identity match or map, an if that rebuilds the boolean it tested, a variable read once on the next line, a two-call pipeline one library call replaces, an await on a promise returned anyway, and an immediately invoked wrapper around code that could run directly.
invariant: Every step of an expression must affect the value the expression produces.

relations.label: reaches the same value without the step

legitimate: The step stays when it changes something: an await inside a try block that must catch the rejection, a binding that names an opaque sub-expression or is reused, an identity clause written for exhaustiveness, and an IIFE that creates a scope the module cannot give.

name: Circular module dependency
rationale: Each rule flags modules that depend on each other in a cycle, through value imports, re-exports, or function-level imports used to hide the cycle from analysis.
invariant: Modules must form an acyclic dependency graph, and a cycle must not be hidden behind a deferred import.
legitimate: Rule 089 belongs here only when the function-level import exists to hide a cycle; a deferred import is correct for an optional extra, a heavy SDK kept out of start-up, a platform-specific module, or an import under a type-checking guard.

name: Published surface that is not a contract of its own
rationale: Each rule looks at what a package or service publishes and finds a surface the boundary does not own: a file of re-exports only, a wildcard re-export that republishes whatever its target holds, a service handing back its persistence entity, and an exported signature naming a type the package keeps private.
invariant: What a boundary publishes must be an enumerated set of names that the boundary owns and that consumers can reach.

relations.label: exposes or inherits its contents from

legitimate: A facade package defined as the union of submodules released together can re-export them wholesale, an internal barrel used only inside the repository carries little of this cost, and a persistence type is fine where it is itself the published contract.

name: Shared abstraction grown a branch per caller
rationale: The rule flags a shared abstraction that has accumulated a branch for each caller's special case, so it now costs more than the duplication it removed.
invariant: A shared abstraction must fit its callers without caller-specific branches; when the branching exceeds the duplication it removed, the abstraction must be re-inlined.
legitimate: A bounded, principled set of configuration options is not special-casing; the fault is an unbounded growth of caller-specific branches.

name: Test count against a budget
rationale: The rule selects a test suite for review when its count exceeds twice the number of distinct behaviors; quantity alone does not show which tests are redundant.
invariant: A test suite should hold the tests its behaviors need and no more.
legitimate: Many distinct edge cases of one behavior, or legitimately broad behavior coverage, can exceed a raw count.

name: Effects hidden from the call site
rationale: Each rule flags a function whose mutation, I/O, dependency acquisition or control flow is invisible at its call boundary: a getter with side effects, hidden parameter mutation, a query that also commands, a service locator, validation that throws as control flow, and effects buried in opaque delegates.
invariant: A function's name and signature must reveal its effects; a query must not mutate and a command must not masquerade as a query.

relations.label: can see at the call site

legitimate: The effect is the function's named, documented purpose, or it is transparent to the caller, such as caching that preserves semantics.

name: Interposed unit that only forwards
rationale: Across functions, modules, classes, components and layers, these rules flag a unit that sits between a consumer and a provider and passes its payload along unchanged: pass-through wrappers, async functions with nothing to await, field-copying adapters, classes that only delegate, generic success envelopes, props threaded through components that never read them, and hops between identically shaped DTOs.
invariant: A unit placed between a consumer and a provider must change the data, the contract or the guarantees that pass through it.

relations.label: depends on instead of the provider

legitimate: The hop earns its place when it pins a boundary the consumer must not cross: a stable public surface over a volatile internal one, a seam for a test double or second implementation, or a deprecation alias kept for one release.

name: Variant handled by branching inside one body
rationale: Each rule targets a function that selects among variants with branches inside a shared body: repeated isinstance or equality ladders, if/elif chains without exhaustiveness checking, a boolean flag choosing between two behaviors, and type-tag branches every new variant must extend.
invariant: Variant selection must use a mechanism that states the variant set once and lets a new variant be added without editing existing bodies.
legitimate: The variant set is small, closed and handled at one site, or the ladder is a data-driven mapping that polymorphism would not improve.

name: Test subject replaced by doubles or fixtures
rationale: Each rule flags a test whose pass is produced by substitutes for the production code: the unit's own methods are stubbed, its internal collaborators or value objects are patched, no production function is called, or a fixture produces the state the assertion reads. The green signal comes from the test's scaffolding, not from the real unit.
invariant: The result a test asserts on must be produced by executing the production code the test claims to verify, with doubles used only at genuine external boundaries.
legitimate: Doubling a genuine edge (network, clock, filesystem, database, a paid third-party SDK) is the intended use; an interaction test may assert on a double when the outgoing call is itself the specified behavior, and a fixture may build input state as long as the asserted outcome still comes from production code.

name: Assertion that cannot fail on wrong behavior
rationale: These rules ask of a green test whether it would turn red if the code were wrong, and answer no: zero, tautological or swallowed assertions, expected values recomputed the way the implementation computes them or simply incorrect, tests whose subject is a framework or language guarantee, and expected literals whose origin cannot be checked. The assertion does not separate a correct outcome from a relevant incorrect one.
invariant: A test must assert the observable outcome of the project's own code against an expected value derived from the requirement, so that a broken behavior turns the test red.

relations.label: takes its verdict from the produced result of
binds to a correct value derived from the requirement

legitimate: A smoke test that deliberately asserts only that a call does not raise, or a characterization test that pins current output before a refactor, is weak by design and fine when the suite does not count it as behavioral evidence; a test of framework behavior is justified when the project configured the framework in a way that can regress; a self-evident literal (HTTP 404, the length of a visible fixture list) needs no derivation comment.

name: Verification disabled or weakened to keep the suite green
rationale: These rules watch edits to the test suite rather than to the product: assertions lowered or removed, expectations rewritten to match what the implementation now returns, tests skipped or ignored, and skip markers left after their reason expired. The suite result survives with less evidence behind it.
invariant: A test the suite counts must run and keep the strength it had, unless the specified behavior itself changed; a failing test is fixed, not disabled or weakened.

relations.label: lowers the assertion or stops it running

legitimate: A skip with a live reason is proper practice: a feature not yet implemented, a platform the runner lacks, a known upstream bug with a ticket. An expectation changed because the specification changed is also proper.

name: Verdict decided by elapsed time or leftover state
rationale: These rules flag tests whose outcome is settled by something other than the behavior they exercise: a fixed sleep or spin in place of waiting on a condition, and global or nonlocal state carried from one test to the next. A green run records that scheduling or test order was favorable, and the race or missing reset stays hidden.
invariant: A test's verdict must depend only on the behavior it exercises, starting from the state its own setup establishes and synchronizing on observable conditions rather than assumed delays.

relations.label: waits on an observable condition of
decides the verdict by how long it waited
decides the verdict by which test ran first

legitimate: Sleeping is correct when elapsed time is the behavior under test (a cache TTL, a debounce window, a rate limiter) with an explicit tolerance; shared fixtures are correct when they are read-only or reset between tests.

name: Test bound to internal structure, not observable behavior
rationale: These rules describe tests written to the shape of the implementation: assertions on calls into internal helpers, per-method test classes mirroring production code, and several tests reaching one observable outcome through different private paths. Such tests go red when nothing observable changed and can stay green when the observable result is wrong.
invariant: A test must express its expectation as the result a caller can observe, so that a behavior-preserving refactor cannot change its verdict.

relations.label: asserts the private call path or mirrors its layout
breaks although the outcome is unchanged

legitimate: Asserting a call is correct when the call is the specified behavior (a message published, an audit record written, a request sent to a payment API); per-method tests are correct when each method is itself a public behavior.

name: Redundant tests that add no new verification
rationale: These rules reason about tests that do not add evidence: test functions with identical bodies that differ only in values and should be one parameterized case, and a test count above a per-behavior budget. The count of tests overstates the breadth of behavior verified.
invariant: Each test in a suite must add verification of a behavior that no other test already pins.
legitimate: Repetition is warranted when near-identical tests record separately specified cases (a regression test per reported defect, a table of mandated vectors, a case per locale), or when one behavior has many branches; independent re-verification may be required by a certification standard.

name: Suite omits the contract's boundary and error cases
rationale: Both rules compare the cases a test set exercises with the cases the behavior has to handle: empty and minimum inputs, boundary values, cardinality, illegal events, malformed input, idempotency and the declared error contract. The suite passes while whole input classes never reach the code.
invariant: A suite presented as verifying a behavior must exercise the boundary, empty and error cases that the behavior's contract names, not only the nominal path.

relations.label: is read as covering the whole

legitimate: Cases the type system or a validating framework makes unreachable need no test, and a behavior with no boundary or error branch is fully covered without them; edge cases may also live in a separate file or a parameterized table.

name: Shipped code that no test reaches
rationale: These rules find production artifacts no test touches: a source file unreachable by import from any test, a changed implementation file with no test file, an exported symbol unreachable in the module graph. They establish that verification is absent, not that an existing test gives a false signal.
invariant: Code that a passing suite is taken to vouch for must be reached by at least one test that can fail.

relations.label: reaches from a test entry point
is offered as evidence that the change works

legitimate: Added condition the rules do not check: untested code belongs to Test Slop only when the passing suite is presented as evidence for that code, for instance a change reported as tested or done. Without that claim it is a coverage gap, not a false success signal. Generated code, thin glue, experimental modules and code exercised by an integration suite the import graph cannot see are also acceptable.
kind_condition: the passing suite is presented as evidence that the untested code works, for instance a change reported as tested or done

name: Multi-behavior test selected by name
rationale: The single rule selects a test for review because its name contains "and", read as a sign the test covers more than one behavior. It inspects the name, not the body or assertions, so it nominates candidates rather than naming a failure.
invariant: A unit test should pin one behavior, so that a red result names what broke.
legitimate: "and" is often part of one behavior's description (rejects_empty_and_whitespace_input, find_and_replace), and an integration or acceptance test is meant to walk a composite scenario.

name: Unverified narrowing assertion in place of a check
rationale: Each rule catches an expression in which the author asserts a narrower type, a non-null value or a representable range that the compiler cannot prove and no runtime check establishes: `as unknown as X`, `!`, `!!`, `u64 as u32`, `x.(T)` without comma-ok. The compile-time objection is removed by a claim instead of being answered.
invariant: Code may treat a value as a narrower, non-null or range-limited type only when the checker can prove that type or a runtime check establishes it before the use.
roles: value of a wider, nullable or dynamic type
use site that depends on the narrower type

relations.from: use site that depends on the narrower type
relations.to: value of a wider, nullable or dynamic type
relations.label: operates on it as if narrowed

relations.to: value of a wider, nullable or dynamic type
relations.label: establishes the narrower type before use

legitimate: The assertion is sound and the check is elsewhere: a value just validated by a schema parser or a comma-ok branch, a non-null assertion right after a guard the checker cannot follow across a closure or an array index, a cast to the type a test double deliberately violates, or a narrowing conversion whose source range is already bounded by construction.

name: Opaque or top type where the code depends on a structure
rationale: Each rule reports an annotation or cast that gives a value a type with no usable members: `any` or `cast(Any, ...)`, `object`, a bare `dict` return, `Array<any>` or an `any` index signature, `as Record<string, unknown>` on a payload. The value has a structure the surrounding code relies on, but it is written nowhere the checker can use, so the checker stops restricting operations on it.
invariant: A value whose fields or elements the code reads or returns must have that structure named in its declared type, not an opaque top type that admits any shape.
roles: declared or cast-to type of the value

relations.label: depends on specific fields or element types

relations.from: declared or cast-to type of the value
relations.label: names its fields or element type
accepts any member access on it

legitimate: The value genuinely has no structure the code relies on, or the shape is unknown at that point and is narrowed right after: a pass-through logger or cache holding an opaque payload, external JSON received as `unknown` and validated into a typed shape on the next line, a generic serializer or plugin registry, or an interface typed loosely on purpose to mirror a third-party contract that varies.

name: Domain concept left in a primitive type
rationale: Each rule concerns a concept whose legal values are constrained by the domain but which is carried as a plain string or integer, or more generally by a type model that does not express the domain rule: a `str` status parameter, a raw primitive for a mode or kind, the same handful of string literals compared across files, a type that leaves business invariants unencoded. The type the checker sees admits values the domain forbids.
invariant: A domain concept with a constrained set of legal values or states must be given a type that excludes the values and states outside that set.
roles: domain concept with a constrained value set
parameter, field or type model carrying it

relations.to: parameter, field or type model carrying it
relations.label: passes one member of the set

relations.from: parameter, field or type model carrying it
relations.to: domain concept with a constrained value set
relations.label: encodes which values are legal
accepts a value the domain rejects

legitimate: The value set is not closed or not owned here: free text, an identifier or key whose values come from outside; a string passed straight through to a protocol or external API that defines the vocabulary; a boundary layer that accepts the wire string and converts it once to the typed value; a repeated literal that is a message or a path rather than a member of a domain set; an early prototype whose domain model is still being found.

name: Dispatch over a closed variant set with exhaustiveness unenforced
rationale: Both rules concern a branch over the members of a closed set written so that the compiler cannot see the set as covered: a `match`/`switch` whose default arm does not assert the impossible case, and an `isinstance`/enum `if`/`elif` chain that simply runs out. What is absent is the compile-time objection when a variant is added.
invariant: Where code branches over a closed set of variants, adding a variant must make the dispatch a type error until it is handled.

relations.label: handles every variant that exists today
turns an uncovered variant into a type error
accepts the dispatch that ignores it

legitimate: The set is open by design, so there is nothing to be exhaustive over: dispatch on a type hierarchy third parties extend, on a value parsed from input where the default arm is the real error path, or a chain whose final branch is a documented general case that stays correct for any new member. The rules do not check that the set is closed.
kind_condition: the set of variants being dispatched over is closed (a discriminated union or exhaustive enum), not an open hierarchy or externally defined value set

name: Check suppressed instead of satisfied
rationale: Each rule finds a place where a type, lint or build check the project runs was switched off rather than satisfied: an inline directive (`@ts-ignore`, `# type: ignore`, `# noqa`, `eslint-disable`), a suppression attribute or unmatched pragma, a build-file element that clears warnings or nullability, or an edit to the checker's own configuration file. The flagged code is left as it was and the waiver carries no visible, bounded reason.
invariant: A diagnostic that an adopted check reports must be fixed in the code, or waived only with the reason recorded and the waiver confined to the code it excuses; the check itself must not be loosened to make the code pass.
roles: suppression directive, build setting or config edit

relations.from: suppression directive, build setting or config edit
relations.label: cancels or loosens its verdict while the code stands

relations.to: suppression directive, build setting or config edit
relations.label: states the reason and bounds the scope

legitimate: A waiver that is both explained and narrow: a `@ts-expect-error` naming the upstream issue, a `# type: ignore[attr-defined]` with a comment pointing at a wrong stub, `#[expect(dead_code, reason = "...")]`, a `NoWarn` for one analyser ID in generated code with the reason in the file. For a configuration edit (rule 332), it is this failure only when the edit removes or weakens a rule the current change was failing; adopting a configuration, tightening a rule, or fixing a path or glob is legitimate.

name: Declared cross-boundary type contradicted by the payload
rationale: The rule finds a type that one component declares for data another component sends, where the two disagree: the producer wraps the payload in an envelope and the consumer type describes the unwrapped body. The declaration is not merely imprecise but false, and nothing validates the payload against it, so the error shows only when the data arrives.
invariant: A type declared for data crossing a component boundary must describe the shape the producing side actually sends, and something must check that it does.

relations.label: returns it in its own envelope
checks it against the declared type

legitimate: The declared type is kept in sync with the producer by a shared schema or generated client, or a runtime validator parses the payload at the boundary; or the declared type covers only part of the payload on purpose, or a typed adapter between the two sides does the unwrapping.

name: Published signature resting on a type that is not part of the contract
rationale: Both rules look at a signature a consumer must use from outside and find in it a type never published for that boundary: an ORM entity returned where a response DTO belongs, or a type referenced by an export but not exported itself. The consumer receives a contract it cannot properly name or rely on, because the type belongs to the provider's interior.
invariant: Every type that appears in a signature across a public boundary must be a type defined, exported and published as part of that boundary's contract.

relations.label: calls it from outside the boundary
is declared and published as part of it
hands it an interior type it cannot name or rely on

legitimate: The boundary is internal, so the interior type is the contract: a package's own modules calling each other, a layered application that deliberately shares its domain model between service and transport, a type exported through another entry point or re-export the check does not follow, or a read model whose entity shape the API documents as its response.

name: Escape-hatch annotation ratio per file
rationale: The rule names no defective construct: it counts a file's annotations, counts how many are escape hatches (`Any`, `any`, `interface{}`, `dynamic`, `object`, `dyn Any`), and reports the file when the share passes thirty per cent with at least five annotations. It selects code for review by a ratio.
invariant: Escape-hatch annotations should be the exception in a typed file, not its ordinary vocabulary.

relations.label: make up more than thirty per cent of them
selects it for review without naming a defect

legitimate: Files where loose types are the subject matter: serialisation and dynamic dispatch layers, a foreign-function or plugin boundary, generic container and reflection utilities, adapters over untyped third-party libraries, where every annotation can be justified while the ratio is far above the threshold.
